references.text: Jacob offers to serve Laban for seven years in order to have Rachel as his wife, which shows his deep love for her.
The Lord sees that Leah is less loved than Rachel and opens her womb while Rachel remains barren, illustrating the consequences of Jacob's greater love for Rachel.
Rachel becomes jealous of Leah because she is barren, even though Jacob loves her most—a direct result of the favoritism described in Gen 29:30.
Jacob mentions that he has served Laban for twenty years—fourteen years for his two daughters—which confirms the additional seven years he worked for Rachel.
The law concerning the birthright when a man has two wives, one loved and one unloved, reflects the situation between Rachel and Leah.
Completion of the promise of seven years of work for Rachel; it shows the contrast between how love perceives time and the actual effort involved.
The source of the promise of seven years of work; it illustrates the connection between Jacob's love and his willingness to labor.
The event that triggered the second seven-year period; it shows the causal link between Leah's night and Jacob's continued work.
